title: AI won't break SAP, but it will shatter seat-based pricing
dek: AI won't flatten what enterprise software has accumulated, but it will shatter seat-based pricing. SAP's defense isn't training its own foundation model — it's open partnerships plus business understanding. The real battlefield is the last mile: process, data and organizational inertia.
why: A rare view from an executive inside a legacy enterprise software giant, using concrete numbers and cases to puncture the illusion that "the model is the product" — and explaining why 28% of attempts yield only 3% in returns.
who: Enterprise software founders, investors, heads of technology at companies going global, and engineers trying to figure out whether FDE is a good career direction.

points.h: The real disruption is the pricing model
points.body: AI's impact on SAP isn't at the code layer, it's in the business model. SAP's stock fell from a high of $300 to $160, but stretched out to 2021 it still grew more than 20%; Adobe dropped from about 480 to around 220, and Zoom has almost vanished. What's actually being replaced is point-solution SaaS. The core of the shock is the traditional seat-based pricing model, which will shift toward consumption-based or even outcome-based pricing — a challenge every enterprise software company will have to face.

points.h: Don't train a foundation model — stay open
points.body: SAP doesn't train its own general-purpose large model, because foundation models evolve too fast and what SAP is good at is enterprise process, data and interaction. SAP's approach is to open up to all third-party models, and on model selection, pair the most suitable model with the most suitable scenario. At the same time it trains its own proprietary small model, RPT 1.5, on its own structured table data, for financial scenarios like receivables forecasting where accuracy needs to be close to 100% — because in finance, 99% accuracy is still unusable.

points.h: The boss wants AI, but the dirty data is still there
points.body: What big-company CIOs dread most is the boss reading an article on WeChat and forwarding it with "I want that too." The gap is that everyone assumes once AI arrives, the dirty, grubby work no longer has to be done. AI can accelerate data cleaning, but it can't make that process disappear. To land AI, you still need FDEs to comb through historical data and organize it by business object, and at the same time to "distill" the veteran's unstructured decisions into enterprise memory, so that the share that can be automated keeps growing step by step.

points.h: FDE and consultants will eventually merge
points.body: FDE is not a rebranded on-site engineer. Traditional ERP consultants are industry experts who enter from the business side and ultimately land requirements into a standard product; FDEs deploy the people who build the product to the customer ahead of time, and the capability they distill flows back into the product. Early FDEs leaned toward low-level engineering and lacked a converter to turn business needs into coding requirements, which is why Anthropic and OpenAI started partnering with consultancies like McKinsey and Accenture. The two groups will merge into a hybrid role that understands both business and technology — which is exactly the necessary path for spilling out of a small circle into the enterprise market.

A large innovative company built its own agent to handle customs declarations for 33 countries, and accuracy was only 60-70%, so people had to review the remaining errors anyway, to loud complaints. After SAP came in, relying on the GTC global tax platform's basic understanding of 33 countries' tax rules plus document AI's template configuration — replacing long-context tokens — accuracy jumped instantly to the 90s, and what started as a pilot in one country had thirty-plus countries clamoring to go live. This shows that exploring AI's business value doesn't require discarding old accumulation; standard process plus incremental value is the effective path.

McKinsey interviewed more than 2,000 companies worldwide: 28% have already used AI on projects, but only 3% believe there is real business return. So very few projects actually go to production; most are still in POC and prototype stage. Big customers have money to burn on trial and error and move fast; small companies run fast with open-source tools; those struggling most are mid-sized companies in the few-hundred-million to roughly 10-billion range, where whether to embrace AI is strongly correlated with the founder's mindset — and Chinese companies are more willing to put money into the product side than the management side.

points.h: Going global rides on a localization base
points.body: SAP's global platform itself covers operations in more than 150 countries, and its product organization includes a localization team dedicated to tax compliance localization for each country. Chinese companies going global can borrow this base directly and only worry about their business. Lenovo has worked with SAP from 20 billion to several hundred billion in scale, and now uses process mining tools to comb through more than 2,000 processes to find breakpoints and room for efficiency gains. When acquiring European companies, the other side is naturally an SAP user, so system integration has a built-in advantage.

quotes.text: You can't escape handling the enterprise's process, organization and data; you can't escape understanding the customer's business; you can't escape how I turn business into my code. It still needs a human in the loop to intervene.
I think it's not that it doesn't exist — it's just that the patterns of history tell us that spillover takes time.
The boss often reads something on WeChat about what AI can do, then forwards it and says "I want that too" — that's the biggest headache for CIOs right now, especially at big companies.

Because after all, most of your current business still follows certain rules. You just need to, on top of a well-laid foundation, fill in the parts that used to be less standardized, that you couldn't read, or that were very costly to collect — that's actually a very good state.
Right now the whole AI world is one big world of coopetition, a big melee. Yes — nobody can do without anybody else, but at the same time everyone wants to carve out a piece of land for themselves.
For enterprises it's actually a relatively complicated thing — you play the game, you pay the price.
